concepts.title: Transgenic Plants via Agrobacterium and Biolistics

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Transgenic Plants via Agrobacterium and Biolistics' refers to.
questions.a: Transgenesis plants a foreign gene and watches it pass to progeny: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, the natural genetic engineer, donates its Ti plasmid T-DNA once tumor genes are disarmed and swapped for genes of interest plus markers; where dicots yield to this vector, cereals take DNA bullets instead - gold or tungsten particles shot by a gene gun - and protoplasts accept naked DNA helped by PEG or electric pulses, feeding crops like Bt cotton, grown commercially in India since 2002, along with herbicide-tolerant and virus-resistant varieties.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Transgenic Plants via Agrobacterium and Biolistics'.
questions.a: Disarm the T-DNA, load your gene, and let the bacterium or a gene gun carry it past the plant cell wall.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Transgenic Plants via Agrobacterium and Biolistics' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Transgenic Animals and Molecular Pharming' refers to.
questions.a: Animal pharming turns livestock into bioreactors: pronuclear microinjection into the larger male pronucleus, embryonic stem-cell transfer through the blastocyst inner cell mass, or single-copy retroviral insertion build the transgenics - Tracy the ewe secreted alpha1-antitrypsin in milk, Rosie the 1997 cow enriched milk with human alpha-lactalbumin, and goat-made ATryn won FDA approval in 2009 - while chimeric mice and GEAC oversight frame the research and its ethics.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Transgenic Animals and Molecular Pharming'.
questions.a: Inject, electrify or infect the embryo, then harvest the human protein from milk - with regulators watching the ethics.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Transgenic Animals and Molecular Pharming' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Gene Therapy Approaches and Delivery' refers to.
questions.a: Gene therapy repairs faulty genes by delivering correct copies - the 1990 ADA-SCID treatment of a four-year-old girl set the precedent - through three strategies: replacement or augmentation of the missing function as with CFTR or p53, inhibition of dominant rogue genes by antisense means, and CRISPR-Cas9 editing that snips mutations out; delivery runs ex vivo through cultured cells or in vivo by direct vectors, and only somatic changes stay non-heritable.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Gene Therapy Approaches and Delivery'.
questions.a: Replace, silence or edit - and choose ex vivo convenience or in vivo directness, remembering germ-line edits are heritable.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Gene Therapy Approaches and Delivery' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Recombinant Vaccines from Subunit to mRNA

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Recombinant Vaccines from Subunit to mRNA' refers to.
questions.a: Recombinant vaccines trade whole pathogens for precision: live genetically modified or vector-based vaccines such as recombinant vaccinia carrying about 200 genes' worth of foreign antigens; subunit vaccines brewing hepatitis B surface antigen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae since the 1987 Recombivax licence; DNA vaccines shot into muscle by gene gun; and mRNA vaccines wrapped in lipid nanoparticles that powered COVID-19 responses alongside Covaxin and Covishield, with edible banana-based HBsAg vaccines on the horizon.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Recombinant Vaccines from Subunit to mRNA'.
questions.a: Deliver only the antigen gene or its message - safer than live pathogen, faster to update for new variants.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Recombinant Vaccines from Subunit to mRNA' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Monoclonal Antibodies by Hybridoma Technology' refers to.
questions.a: Koehler and Milstein's 1975 hybridoma trick fuses short-lived antibody-producing B plasma cells with immortal myeloma cells using polyethylene glycol; HAT medium kills unfused myelomas and aged B cells alike so only hybridomas endure, secreting monoclonal antibodies aimed at one epitope - later humanised with mouse-human chimeric segments for therapy, diagnostics like pregnancy kits and tumor-targeted drug delivery.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Monoclonal Antibodies by Hybridoma Technology'.
questions.a: Fuse mortality with immortality: only the B-cell-and-myeloma hybrid survives HAT medium and keeps secreting one specific antibody.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Monoclonal Antibodies by Hybridoma Technology' taught, and from which source text?
